items: Setting up new clients or suppliers

blocks.content: I do not sell software licences, and I do not replace your team. Where I can, the systems I build work with the tools you already use.
You hear about changes while there is still time to act on them.
My own system reads UK company records, insolvency notices and public contract awards every night, and reports changes the same morning.
A system for your business would read the sources that matter in your market.

blocks.content: A system rarely removes a task completely. It usually takes the routine part and leaves a person to check the result. Expect most of the time back, not all of it.
Five situations I see often. Each one is an illustration of a common pattern, not a named client. Each page shows what happens today, what I would build and what changes.

items.title: The Monday report
items.description: Wholesale, 40 staff. Most of a morning every week, rebuilding the same report from three systems.

blocks.content: This one already runs: my own system reads these public records every night. The business below is an illustration.

blocks.kicker: Illustration, using a system that runs today
blocks.title: Today

blocks.content: A distributor buys most of its stock from one supplier. Nobody watches that supplier's public records.
The supplier's accounts become overdue at Companies House. Then a winding-up petition appears in The Gazette. The distributor finds out when deliveries stop.
You give the system a list of the companies you depend on: suppliers, large customers and partners. Each night it checks their filings and notices.
When something changes, you get one short email that says what changed and where to see it.
Weeks of warning instead of none. That is time to find a second supplier, change payment terms, or speak to the customer first.
A list of company names or company numbers. Nothing needs to connect to your own systems.
A wholesaler with 40 staff holds a leadership meeting every Monday at 11. This is an illustration of a common pattern.
The operations manager starts at 8. Sales figures come from the accounts system, stock levels from the warehouse system, and delivery times from the courier's website.
Each one is exported, pasted into a spreadsheet and tidied. The report is ready just before the meeting. By then the figures are a day old, and nobody has had time to check them.
Overnight, the system collects the same figures from the same three places. It builds the report in the format the meeting already uses.
If a figure looks wrong, for example stock falling to zero overnight, it is flagged at the top of the report.

items.label: hours a week back for the operations manager

blocks.content: The manager spends Monday morning on what the figures mean, not on collecting them.
Read access to the three systems, a copy of the current report, and one person to compare the first new reports with the old ones. The new report runs alongside the old one until the two match.
A professional services firm with 25 staff takes on about 30 new clients a month. This is an illustration of a common pattern.
When a proposal is signed, an administrator copies the client's details into the customer database (CRM), the billing system and the project tracker.
Then they email the account lead, finance and the delivery team. It takes about 40 minutes a client. Most months, at least one client is set up with a wrong address or a missing contact.
Signing the proposal starts it. The system creates the records in all three systems and checks that nothing is missing.
If something is missing, it asks a named person to fill it in. Only then does it tell the team.

items.label: hours a month back, at 30 new clients

blocks.content: Missing details are caught before anyone starts work, not when the first invoice bounces.
Access to the three systems and a list of the details each one needs. Also an hour with the person who does this today, to see how it really works.
A building services company bids for public contracts. This is an illustration of a common pattern.
Someone checks the main tender websites when they have time, usually once a week. A council publishes a planned contract months in advance, but nobody sees that early notice.
By the time the tender opens, a competitor has already met the buyer twice and helped shape the brief.
A system reads the public contract notices every night, including the early notices that come before a tender.
It keeps the ones that match your work and your region, and sends a short summary each morning.
You hear about the work at the planning stage, while the buyer is still open to conversations.
A description of the work you want and where. In the first weeks, a person marks which notices were useful, so the matching gets better.
A family business of 15 people is run by its founder. This is an illustration of a common pattern.
Every morning the owner checks the orders, approves discounts, decides which jobs go first and chases late payers. None of it is written down.
The owner has not taken two weeks off in six years. Money is not the reason. Nobody else knows how the decisions are made.
First I sit with the owner and write down the checks and decisions, with the reasons. Most of them turn out to be rules, such as a small discount for repeat customers.
The system makes the routine decisions by those rules. It sends the unusual ones to a named person, with the facts needed to decide.
The business keeps running while the owner is away. Because the rules are written down, new staff are easier to train.
Time with the owner to walk through a normal week, and a second person who will handle the unusual cases.

label: How a new system is tested

blocks.content: A new system never starts by running alone. It moves through four stages, one at a time.
At each stage you can see what it did and why. It moves up only after its results have been right for long enough. If mistakes start to rise, it moves back a stage by itself.

blocks.text: In Callsheet, my own directory, two of the three tasks that may run alone have reached the last stage. I still check the third.

blocks.content: Callsheet is a public directory of UK film, TV and media companies. I built it alone, and it runs without staff.
Its jobs range from nightly checks of public records to quarterly reviews of its own categories. My part is reading one summary a week.

blocks.label: Sources my system reads every night

blocks.content: Each night my system reads these public sources and links them. A change in one can point to a risk or an opportunity in another.
Every project follows the same four steps, in this order. You can stop after the summary and keep it.

Tell me which job takes up your team's week. The first call is 30 minutes and free.
Afterwards you get a one-page summary of where time is lost and what I would automate first. It is yours to keep, whether or not we work together.
There is no sales pitch. If I do not find anything worth automating, I will say so.
